The authors have studied the prevalence estimates of MSD among dental healthcare workers using a systematic search of five databases. The authors observed high prevalence of MSD among dental healthcare workers which highlights the importance of them becoming aware of and adopting appropriate ergonomic postures early in their careers in order to reduce work-related MSD.

The paper is well written and covers most of the aspects in this issue. There are a few suggestions below:

Were the two reviewers calibrated before doing the search? If possible the authors can provide the kappa statistics for agreement between the two reviewers.
                    The authors can provide the numbers of hits with each of the five databases in the prisma flowchart.
                    The authors can provide the years included in the search. Also if there was any manual search carried out in addition to the automated search.

Thanks for the opportunity to read this interesting paper. I think it is a useful idea to apply this same 'user testing' method to the challenge of improving diversity of clinical trial recruitment. I have a few major/general and a few minor comments all for your consideration, below.

Major/general: 
                Method, procedure for testing original…: it seems individuals' understanding was assessed by just one person. Could you give more detail about what quality control was in place around this to ensure consistency of ratings? This seems quite critical to your study's results.
                    It seems the 'original' information sheet did not adhere to already-existing best practice about information sheet design, given your revisions included use of lay language, removing technical terms, use of illustrations. What's the justification of using that as the comparator? Did you consider starting from an information sheet that adheres to best practice and then improving it further?
                    The section on ethical approval says the study received 'retrospective ethical approval'; this seems to imply it was conducted without ethical approval. Could some more explanation be provided around this, please?
                    The UK Health Research Authority has recently released new guidance/expectations around patient information sheets - I think your work needs to take account of this more (including the bits about policy and ethics implications in the discussion). Minor: 
                Abstract: the point made about people from ethnic minorities having higher rates of mental health problems and being less likely to take part in research is important. However, I didn't see this covered in the main paper itself and suggest it should be added (with suitable references).
                    Introduction: some of the references refer to reports about the effect of information sheet changes on trial recruitment. There is an argument that there is an important distinction between redesigning information sheets to improve recruitment vs improving quality of decision-making. The ELICIT study defined a core outcome set for studies about informed consent, and eventually excluded recruitment from their set. I wonder if your paper should address this tension, perhaps with reference to ELICIT?
                    Table 1: it is unclear whether this table shows results of a systematic search for relevant prior papers, or is just a convenience sample of known results?
                    Table 1: in all rows apart from the third one, the 'general population' is the sum of the number of individuals involved in all the testing rounds. Is this deliberate or should row 3 be updated?
                    Table 1: Parker et al in the column 'PIS revision' - currently says 'PIB was re-written…' - should this be PIS?
                    Table 1: do any of the reports include p-values or other measures to help interpret the strength of the evidence?
                    Introduction, final paragraph: 'the method can support the inclusion of ethnic minorities…' - please provide references for this claim, or soften it.
                    Method, study design: there is a general statement about why randomised trials are not always possible, but it is not clear why randomisation is not possible in this particular instance (e.g. is it also about 'high cost' here?)
                    Method, study design: the sentence about non-randomised independent between-groups design is duplicated.
                    Method, Table 2: why were the eligibility criteria for this study not the same as those for the trial?
                    Method: it's good that the process was done in Urdu and English, but I don't think it's clear how you decided which one in each case. Was this purely by participant preference?
                    Figure 3: what do the annotated numbers mean?
                    Method, paragraph 'YM and WW' - 'the original PIS was initially screened and reviewed in detail' - by whom? And was this one in English or do you mean the English and translated versions?
                    Same paragraph: 'a consensus was reached' - by whom?
                    Method, paragraph 'Later, Urdu translation' - typo on line 4 'om the initial translation by MN'; and who is MN?
                    Method, Data analysis: 'based on the participant's ability to find each of the 19 key questions…' - I'm not sure it's clear how the 'ability to find' was assessed. And is this the same as the 'reading time' measurement?
                    Method, Data analysis: text in article says 'REF needed' - presumably still needs filling in.
                    Results, comprehension time: I suggest 'there was a significant difference' should say 'statistically significant difference'.
                    Same paragraph: 'mean difference 3.84' - 3.84 what?
                    Next paragraph: 'questions under the categories of nature and purpose… had significant problems'. Could you be more precise than just 'significant problems'? Does it mean very few participants found those topics?
                    Table 5: please add units to the column 'mean'
                    Table 5: I am not a trained statistician, but just to check - a rule of thumb I would usually expect to see is that if a p-value is below 0.05 then the 95% confidence intervals would not overlap. However, in the comprehension rows they do appear to overlap. Are the numbers correct?
                    Results, general: again, I am not a trained statistician, but based on my experience working with statisticians, I wonder about the use of p-values as reported - given the study design, small sample size, and multiple testing. It might be more appropriate to report the differences as they are and clearly report the study design and its strengths and limitations, so that readers can decide. I would be interested in others' views (i.e. statisticians) on this, though.

The manuscript entitled, “Patterning ECM microstructure to investigate 3D cellular dynamics under multiplexed mechanochemical guidance”, outlines the development of a platform for 3D cell culture that can modulate chemical and mechanical cues respectively. This novel device can be used to study the relative contribution of chemotaxis and contact guidance on cell morphology and migration.  The ability to independently control fiber alignment vs chemotaxis provides opportunities to address unanswered questions about how these cues impact cell morphology and migration. The utility of the platform is of interest to researchers in this field; however, the manuscript lacks detail in the description of methods and lacks experimental evidence of reproducibility. Addressing these shortcomings is required prior to publication.

1. For a manuscript that defines the development of a novel platform the methodology is extremely vague.    
                As written, it is very unclear how radial vs tangential fiber architecture is achieved.  Some aspects of the mechanical perturbations (rotation of the blade) are provided in the methods section, while some are in the results text. The descriptions of each condition seem to overlap.  Please define both radial and tangential fiber alignment protocols in the methods section. (blade rotation speed, duration of spinning, whether collagen is unpolymerized at the time of spinning, the polymerization conditions, and the exact timing of serum addition vs initiation of image acquisition)   
                Collagen labeling methods are not clear.  The FITC-labeled collagen from AnaSpec is a quenched collagen, which fluoresces upon enzymatic cleavage (MMP activity).  Presumably diluting this collagen into high-concentration Collagen Type I alleviates the quenched fluorescence so that a subset of fibers are fluorescent.  These details should be added to the methods section.   
                The cell concentration is not defined.  “…we suspend cells at low density in neutralized collagen solutions.”  For reproducibility, a cell concentration should be defined.

As written, it is very unclear how radial vs tangential fiber architecture is achieved.  Some aspects of the mechanical perturbations (rotation of the blade) are provided in the methods section, while some are in the results text. The descriptions of each condition seem to overlap.  Please define both radial and tangential fiber alignment protocols in the methods section. (blade rotation speed, duration of spinning, whether collagen is unpolymerized at the time of spinning, the polymerization conditions, and the exact timing of serum addition vs initiation of image acquisition)

Collagen labeling methods are not clear.  The FITC-labeled collagen from AnaSpec is a quenched collagen, which fluoresces upon enzymatic cleavage (MMP activity).  Presumably diluting this collagen into high-concentration Collagen Type I alleviates the quenched fluorescence so that a subset of fibers are fluorescent.  These details should be added to the methods section.

The cell concentration is not defined.  “…we suspend cells at low density in neutralized collagen solutions.”  For reproducibility, a cell concentration should be defined.

2.  It is not clear that the authors have reproduced the alignment conditions.  The experimental N is not reported.  How reproducible is the fiber alignment? Chemical gradients?  The tangential alignment appears quite variable (45-90 degrees), which is a large margin. The analysis of chemical gradients and alignment should be repeated in at least 3 experiments.  Furthermore, were all cell metrics acquired from one device for tangential and one device for radial alignment? Similarly, the migration speeds/distances for radial vs tangential fiber alignment should be repeated across a minimum of 3 independent experiments.

3. The authors state that cellular protrusions are altered between alignment/chemical gradient conditions.  However, images were collected with a 10x objective every hour for 18hrs. Protrusion dynamics in 3D have been reported to occur on the scale of minutes.  Higher magnification and shorter imaging intervals are necessary to ensure that cellular protrusion dynamics are accurately quantified.

4. Finally, if the method is interpreted correctly by this reviewer, the cells are subjected to blade rotation for either 0 or 4 minutes.  The authors do not account for the application of direct mechanical stress on the cells in their response to tangential alignment. This is an important factor that needs to be controlled or minimally discussed.

In this manuscript, Esfahani and Sun described a method to create an experimental platform where cell response to gradient in chemical factors and to the organization of extracellular environment can be decoupled. This is interesting as cells are known to sense and respond to both factors, but the interplay between them is difficult to study systematically. Thus, the approach and the insights obtained from it can be very useful to the community. The work and analyses are solid and were performed nicely, and the manuscript is a pleasure to read. My only suggestions are to include some pertinent missing information, which are crucial for the readers to understand the study. 
                The working mechanism of the device and how it can be used to tune collagen microstructure can be better explained. It is not clear how the blade and boundary condition of the device alone (apparently even without rotation) can already create fiber alignment.
                    The authors state that the value of coherence c is highly affected by noise in the image and therefore can only reach a max value of 0.2 rather than the theoretical 1.0. Some examples of images with different levels of noise and the corresponding c value will be nice (perhaps as a supplementary figure).
                    The authors stated that the tip shape of the blade was optimized to guide the collagen gelation. Since the blade shape appears to be critical to the whole mechanism of the approach, description of the different tip shapes that were tried and the final tip shape and dimensions used will be very useful.
                    It will be great if dimensions are added to the schematic in Figure 1.
                    Since the goal of the study is to study the individual and combined effects of chemotaxis and collagen orientation, it will be most interesting to compare the anisotropic (Figure 3,4) vs. isotropic condition (not included yet) and chemotaxis (Figure 5,6) vs. no chemotaxis (not included yet). Basically including the outcomes of the control conditions.
                    The chemical gradient experiment was done using rhodamine B as a proxy for diffusive factor’s concentration profile. It will be informative to mention the diffusivity and molecular size of rhodamine B as compared to those of chemoattractants normally present in the context of cancer.
                    The chemical gradient experiment was performed only for one condition (isotropic gel), which is different from the conditions used in the rest of the paper (anisotropic gel). It will be more convincing to include results from the anisotropic gels too (those in Figure 3 and in Figure 5).
                    Information about how the chemical gradient experiment was performed is missing in Methods. Also, at what height were the images in Figure 2 taken to analyze the fluorescence intensity?
                    Regarding the experiments described in Figure 4 and 6, as far as I understand the chemical gradient is positive (serum is at the center of the device). So why did the cells move outwards (away from serum) and not inwards (towards serum)? What is the zero position in Figure 4B and 6B?
                    Serum has been previously reported to affect collagen gelation, resulting in different collagen fiber thickness and microstructure. In the presence of serum concentration gradient, could it be that there is also a gradient in collagen fiber formation and microstructure, which could potentially also affect cancer cell migration? If the authors have characterized the collagen at different radial positions, this will be nice to add. Otherwise, at least the authors could comment on this.
